slides.title: ISD 2026 Keynote
slides.body:
> The Great Convergence: Recommendation, Search, and Conversation in Real-World AI Systems

<!-- gap -->

**Pavel Kordík** · ISD 2026 · Prague, 2–4 September

<!-- gap -->

![[fig-affiliation|75%]]
slides.notes: Do not open by introducing yourself: one sentence of who you are, then straight to slide 3. The talk's thesis is on this slide already. Optional 45-second opening scene: one person, one catalogue, four interfaces, one ranked decision.

slides.title: How information retrieval evolved over time?
slides.body:
![[fig-ir-history-convergence|85%]]

***

| **1950s–70s** | **1990s** | **2010s** | **2020s** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retrieve records** | **Rank documents** | **Learn representations** | **Retrieve evidence, compose responses** |
| Boolean retrieval | BM25, PageRank | [word2vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), BERT | RAG, generative search |

***

- Is generative AI part of information retrieval?
- **What exactly is IR in 2026?**
slides.notes: Information retrieval began as matching queries to records, then became ranking at web scale, then representation learning. In the 2020s, systems increasingly retrieve evidence and generate the response, making the system boundary harder to draw. This deck asks what should still count as IR in 2026; if short on time, skip the individual historical examples.
slides.summary: history of information retriaval ... and this deck will answer what is IR in 2026? - is genAI used in IR?

slides.title: Four interfaces, one ranking problem
slides.body:
![[fig-three-interfaces-ranked-items|92%]]

| Search | Recommendation | Conversational retrieval | Agent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Query → ranked pages | User context → ranked items | Dialogue → ranked documents, events … | Goal + permissions → ranked actions, then a constrained execution |

> The interface changes; the decision remains: what should come first?
slides.notes: Show the three mock-ups in the figure and name the fourth interface in the table: an agent acting for the user, which returns at the end of the talk as the newest client of the same pipeline. Search ranks pages, recommendation ranks items, conversational retrieval ranks evidence before composing an answer, an agent ranks actions. If short on time, skip the table and use only the visual and closing line.
slides.summary: Create images of search interface, recommendation interface and conversational retrieval interface to show audiece how it looks like ... ranked items should be present everywhere

slides.title: Four lineages, one operation: rank
slides.body:
![[fig-four-lineages-to-rank|70%]]

| Lineage | What it learned to score | Canonical step |
|---|---|---|
| **Information retrieval** | documents for a query | [Luhn, 1957](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.14.0309) → [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) |
| **Web search** | pages by authority | [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/) |
| **Recommenders** | items for a person | [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905) → [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) |
| **Conversation** | responses, then evidence | [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) |

> Four communities optimised different interfaces and objectives — and each rebuilt the same subroutine: score candidates, sort them, learn from what was shown.
slides.notes: One slide for sixty years: each lineage added a signal it could score — term statistics, links, other people's behaviour, learned sequence context — and every one of them ends in the same operation, a sorted list. The detailed citation tables from the earlier version live here in the notes, not on the screen. If short on time, say only the last line.
slides.summary: Q1 condensed: the four histories in one figure, the citations in the notes.

slides.title: One implementation view: recommendation as retrieval with an implicit query
slides.body:
![[fig-shared-user-embedding-search-recsys|52%]]

| | Search | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Request | user **u** + query **q** | user **u**, **q = ∅** |
| Score | f(**u**, **q**, item) | f(**u**, ∅, item) |
| Where it runs | one model, seven Alipay domains ([Gong et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1145/3583780.3614657)) | same model, same tower |

One frozen text encoder, one vector per item, three consumers: sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering and product search — the design of the [BLaIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03952) benchmark on 571 million Amazon reviews.

> The profile is the query. Alipay is an existence proof, not a theorem: exposure bias, freshness and business constraints still enter on the recommendation side.
slides.notes: Alipay trained one search-and-recommendation foundation model on seven internal datasets: search tasks carry an explicit query, recommendation passes an empty one, and both share the user tower and the item tower. BLaIR shows the same thing at benchmark level: a single embedding table from a frozen language model serves recommendation, CF and search without retraining. If short on time, keep only the table and the last line.
slides.summary: Alipay's production model scores f(user, query, item) for search and sets the query to empty for recommendation; one embedding table feeds retrieval, CF and search in BLaIR.

slides.title: What converged, and what did not
slides.body:
![[fig-convergence-matrix|52%]]

| Increasingly shared by 2026 | Still domain-specific |
|---|---|
| **Representation** — compatible embedding spaces for text, images and IDs, increasingly one shared layer ([CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020), [DPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906)) | **Objective** — relevance vs. engagement vs. task completion; plus freshness, privacy and schema, which never converge |
| **Training signal** — contrastive learning from interactions | **Compute regime** — retrieval scores millions under a millisecond, ranking scores hundreds ([UniPinRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00422)) |
| **Architecture** — Transformer over a token sequence ([HSTU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152)) | **Evaluation** — no shared offline metric; online experiments are the only common ground |

**Counter-evidence, on purpose:** [DLRM](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00091)-style feature-cross rankers and boosted trees still rank in production; BM25 is still a hard zero-shot baseline (BEIR); tuned linear models keep beating newer ones (section V).

> "The backbone architecture has converged; the computational regimes remain distinct." — Pinterest, 2026
slides.notes: This replaces three history slides and one invented percentage from the previous version. The claim the literature supports is narrower and stronger: what merged is the machinery — vectors, contrastive training, transformers — and what did not merge is what the machinery is for and what it costs. Pinterest says it in one sentence in the UniPinRec paper. If short on time, read the two column headers and the quote.
slides.summary: The honest version of the convergence claim: representation, training signal and architecture are shared; objectives, compute regimes, evaluation and economics are not.

slides.title: The shared stack in one picture
slides.body:
![[fig-shared-stack|70%]]

**Catalogue** (items, attributes, data contracts) → **encoders** (text, image, behaviour) → **indexes** (vector, lexical, semantic-ID) → **candidate generation** → **ranker** → **constraints and policies** → **renderer**: a list, a sentence about the list, or an action — and every click flows back as **feedback**.

> Three products, one pipeline — and three different objectives sitting on top of it. The rest of this talk walks down that pipeline and asks what it costs and what it gets wrong.
slides.notes: Anna opens a learning platform: she searches, gets a homepage, asks the assistant a question. All three calls hit the same catalogue, the same encoders, the same candidate generator and the same ranker; only the request and the constraints differ. This is the operational model the audience needs before any mechanism. If short on time, this slide is the one to keep from section I.
slides.summary: Three requests — a query, an empty query, a question — flow through the same boxes: catalogue, encoders, indexes, candidate generation, ranking, constraints, response.

slides.title: The stack converged. The hard questions did not.
slides.body:
![[fig-three-axes-intro|60%]]

| Axis | The question | Where in this talk |
|---|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | does it find the right thing — and how would we know? | mechanisms (II), steering (III), grounding (IV), evaluation (V) |
| **Affordability** | does it fit latency and budget at a hundred million users? | cost, serving, sparse and linear models (VI) |
| **Alignment** | is the "right thing" right for the user, the creator and society? | measurable properties, safety, exposure, judges (VII) — and the agent that asks next (VIII) |

> Shared machinery, three separate bills. Each section pays one of them.
slides.notes: The roadmap the brief promised: after the mechanisms, everything is organised by the three axes named in the annotation — accuracy, affordability, alignment. Say it once here so the audience can place every later slide. If short on time, read the three axis names.
slides.summary: Roadmap: the rest of the talk hangs on the three axes from the annotation.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: Similarity became a dot product
slides.body:
![[fig-two-tower|60%]]

| | Cross-encoder | Two towers |
|---|---|---|
| Most similar pair among 10,000 sentences | 50 million BERT passes, ~65 h on a V100 | 10,000 passes, then vector search — seconds ([Sentence-BERT, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084)) |
| Open-domain QA over Wikipedia | not feasible | 21 M passages in a FAISS index, dot product relevance ([DPR, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906)) |

DPR's finding was the training recipe, not the architecture: in-batch and hard negatives decide the quality of the space.

> Move most model work offline. The online path becomes request encoding, nearest-neighbour search, ranking and constraints.
slides.notes: The mechanism that made convergence possible: move the model work off the request path. A cross-encoder reads query and document together and is unsearchable at scale; a siamese encoder maps each text to a vector, so the catalogue is encoded once and a request costs one encoding plus nearest-neighbour search. Recommenders had shaped their systems this way since matrix factorization — search arrived at the same shape through DPR. If short on time, keep the table.
slides.summary: Sentence-BERT and DPR: a cross-encoder cannot be searched, a siamese encoder can; two towers plus an ANN index is the same shape recommenders had used for years.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: One encoder, three indexes
slides.body:
![[fig-one-encoder-three-indexes|50%]]

| Representation | Index | Example | Where it wins |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dense vector | ANN (FAISS, HNSW) | [DPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906) | semantics, paraphrase |
| Sparse vocabulary weights | inverted index | [SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720): 0.322 vs 0.312 MRR@10 for the dense sibling on MS MARCO | exact terms, existing Lucene stacks |
| Per-token vectors | late interaction | [ColBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832) | precision with offline document encoding |
| All three at once | hybrid sum | [BGE-M3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03216): one forward pass, 8,192 tokens, 100+ languages | one model to operate |

> The backbone may be shared; the index decides what is cheap to retrieve and which errors dominate — missed paraphrases for lexical, missed exact terms for dense.
slides.notes: For an information-systems audience this is the practical consequence of convergence: the representation is fixed by one pretrained encoder, and the retrieval data structure — inverted index, vector index, late interaction — is chosen for the deployment. SPLADE is the striking case: a sparse, Lucene-compatible retriever that slightly beats the dense one trained from the same backbone. If short on time, read only the last two rows.
slides.summary: The same BERT backbone yields dense vectors, sparse vocabulary weights and per-token multi-vectors; the index type becomes a deployment choice.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: Sequences: the NLP toolkit crossed over
slides.body:
![[anim-attention-mechanism|54%]]

| Year | Recommender | Borrowed from NLP | The trick |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2016 | [GRU4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06939) | GRU (seq2seq translation) | a session is a sentence, the next click is the next word |
| 2018 | [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) | causal self-attention | the same block, item IDs in place of words |
| 2019 | [BERT4Rec](https://doi.org/10.1145/3357384.3357895) | masked-token objective | Cloze over the interaction sequence |
| 2024 | [HSTU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) | generative modelling, scaling laws | a user's actions as a token stream, 1.5 trillion parameters |

> "Actions speak louder than words" — and they are modelled with the same machine.
slides.notes: Each row transplants the sequence-modelling blocks from language modelling with item identifiers in place of words; what changed is the data-generating process and the objective — implicit feedback, exposure bias, a non-stationary vocabulary. Meta's HSTU closes the loop by showing that the scaling law of language models holds for recommendation once the task is written as sequence transduction. If short on time, read the first and the last row.
slides.summary: GRU4Rec took the GRU from machine translation, SASRec took self-attention, BERT4Rec took the masked objective; items became tokens, the user became a sentence.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: Product and site search borrow recommender machinery
slides.body:
![[fig-alipay-unified|56%]]

| System | What is shared | Reported effect |
|---|---|---|
| Alipay S&R foundation model ([CIKM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1145/3583780.3614657)) | user tower, item tower, frozen language model for text | one model across seven search and recommendation domains, aimed at cold start |
| Pinterest [PinFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704) (RecSys 2025) — recommendation-side evidence | one 20-billion-parameter user-activity backbone pretrained once, fine-tuned per surface | serving throughput +600 % from a deduplicated attention kernel; API latency −7 % |
| [BLaIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03952) benchmark | one item-embedding table | consumed by sequential recommendation, CF and product search |

> In logged-in commerce, news and super-apps, search is a recommender with a query attached. Public web search is a different, more constrained animal.
slides.notes: Three scales of the same statement: a benchmark, a payments super-app and a visual discovery platform all put search and recommendation on one representation. The numbers worth quoting are Pinterest's, because they are about serving, not accuracy: a foundation model was affordable only after a kernel gave six times the throughput. If short on time, keep the Pinterest row and the closing line.
slides.summary: Q2 evidence: one backbone serves search and recommendation at Alipay and Pinterest; the same embeddings feed both at benchmark level.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: RAG is retrieval and ranking with a writer at the end
slides.body:
![[fig-rag-is-retrieval|60%]]

| Fusion | Where the evidence enters | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Query-based** | text prepended to the prompt | simplest; costs context tokens |
| **Logits-based** | mixed into the output distribution | keeps the prompt short; needs model access |
| **Latent** | cross-attention over retrieved vectors | cheapest per token; training required |
| **Parametric** | baked into weights | no retrieval at request time; stale |

Taxonomy from the [RAG survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13193); the retrieval and ranking stages are the ones from the previous slides.

> The most controllable place to choose evidence is retrieval and reranking. The generator still has to be checked for faithfulness.
slides.notes: For this audience RAG is best introduced as the pipeline they already saw, with one extra stage: a language model writes a sentence about the top-ranked items. The four fusion styles matter because they are the affordability knob — query-based fusion is the one everyone starts with and the most expensive per request. If short on time, keep the figure and the last line.
slides.summary: Q3: the mechanism of retrieval-augmented generation, and the four ways retrieved evidence can be fused into the model.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: Items become tokens: semantic IDs and constrained decoding
slides.body:
![[fig-semantic-ids|44%]]

1. **Encode** each item's content → a vector.
2. **Quantise** with residual codebooks → a tuple such as ⟨12, 23, 8⟩: coarse category first, detail last.
3. **Generate** the next tuple from the user's sequence with a Transformer ([TIGER, NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065)).
4. **Constrain** the beam search to a prefix trie, so every decoded tuple is an existing item.

Beauty benchmark: up to **+29 % NDCG@5** over SASRec. New items get an ID from their content, so ranking them without history becomes possible; how well depends on content quality, code stability and the ranker.

What the trie does **not** guarantee: relevance, stock, safety, or a stable ID when the catalogue churns and codes collide — those remain ranking and operations problems.

> Guard rails for generation are not a policy document. They are a trie.
slides.notes: This is the slide that connects to the other keynotes: Klímek's structured, machine-readable catalogue is the precondition, and Mannaert's guard rails for generation have an exact counterpart here — constrained decoding makes it impossible for the model to name an item that does not exist. Semantic IDs are also why generative retrieval handles cold start: an item's identifier is computed from its content. If short on time, keep the four steps and the last line.
slides.summary: TIGER: quantise the content embedding into a short code, train a seq2seq model to generate the next code, decode only through a prefix trie of real items.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: Conversation ranks items too
slides.body:
**GLIDE** (Spotify, 2026, [arXiv:2603.17540](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17540)) — the model reads *user, listening history, instruction* and writes the semantic IDs of shows, in order: `p(SID(show) | prompt(user, history, instruction))`

| 21-day A/B test on the Home surface | |
|---|---|
| Non-habitual podcast streams | **+5.4 %** |
| New-show discovery | **+14.3 %** |
| Engagement, satisfaction | no regression, within production cost and latency |

> The interface is a sentence. The output is still a ranked list of catalogue items.
slides.notes: The cleanest production evidence that conversational recommendation is ranking: the model receives an instruction and a long-term user embedding as a soft prompt, and decodes semantic IDs — catalogue items — in order. The metric Spotify optimised is discovery of shows the listener does not already follow. If short on time, read the two percentages and the last line.
slides.summary: Spotify's GLIDE treats podcast discovery as instruction following over a discretised catalogue: the answer to a sentence is a ranked list of semantic IDs.

slides.group: II · How the walls came down
slides.title: Some cascades are being compressed into one model
slides.body:
![[fig-onerec|58%]]

| System | What it replaced | Numbers reported |
|---|---|---|
| **OneRec**, Kuaishou ([tech report, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695)) | the four-stage cascade | 25 % of QPS; App Stay Time +0.54 % / +1.24 %; operating expense **10.6 %** of the old pipeline, as reported — migration cost not included |
| **UniPinRec**, Pinterest ([2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00422)) | separate retrieval and ranking models | Hit@3 +14.8 % offline, ~+1 % online; latency **−11.1 %**, QPS **+63.6 %** |
| **UniSearch**, Kuaishou (2025) | the search cascade: recall, pre-rank, rank | generative search deployed in Kuaishou live and short-video search; offline Recall@300 63.5 → 67.5 |

> Same stack, now also for search. Most production systems still run a cascade — but notice which numbers got these three deployed.
slides.notes: The production convergence in three rows. OneRec is the headline because of the cost line: an end-to-end generative model at ten times the FLOPs of the cascade, yet 10.6 % of its operating expense, because a single model uses the hardware — the report gives 23.7 % and 28.8 % model-FLOPs utilisation in training and inference. Pinterest kept its funnel and unified two stages; the offline lift shrank tenfold online but latency and throughput improved, which is what shipped it. If short on time, read only the last column. Bridge to the next section: once four interfaces share one stack, user control has to move from interface tricks into the representation itself — which is where steering by language comes in.
slides.summary: OneRec, UniPinRec and UniSearch replace retrieve → pre-rank → rank with one model, in production, with the cost and latency numbers that made it possible.

slides.title: You cannot edit your own vector
slides.body:
| How you steer a recommender today | What it touches |
|---|---|
| Filters, boosters, business rules | the candidate list, after scoring |
| Prompting an LLM recommender ([P5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13366), 2022) | the text interface; collaborative signal is weak in warm catalogues |
| Instruction over semantic IDs ([GLIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17540), 2026) | the generator, at Spotify scale |
| Profile editors, explicit likes, critiquing | the interface again; the learned representation is untouched |
| **Changing the user embedding itself** | the model's internal state — the subject of the next three slides |

<!-- gap -->

> Existing controls sit outside the learned user representation. The question: can a sentence edit that representation directly?
slides.notes: The gap the thesis addresses: controllable recommendation existed at the interface level — rules, prompts, instructions, critiquing — while the collaborative-filtering user embedding itself stayed untouched. Jaroslav Hradil's thesis, supervised by Rodrigo Alves in our lab with Recombee compute, gives one concrete way to steer that representation with language, evaluated offline across four backbones. Do not claim priority from the stage. If short on time, read the last row and the quote.
slides.summary: Q4 opener: every recommender represents the user as a vector nobody can read or change; the ways to steer so far sit on top of the model, not inside it.

slides.title: Unfold the vector: sparse autoencoders make a profile legible
slides.body:
![[fig-steering-pipeline|52%]]

1. Train any collaborative-filtering backbone (ALS, ELSA, LightGCN, two-tower) and expose `encode(interactions) → e` and `decode(e) → scores`.
2. Train a **TopK sparse autoencoder** on the dense user embeddings: wider latent (2–8×), ReLU, keep the k largest activations (k = 16 or 32).
3. The sparse code is the steerable interface: one dense dimension that meant "sci-fi + documentary + adventure" becomes three separate neurons.

Reconstruction check (thesis, Figure 5.1): with the latent fixed at 4,096 and k rising, the recommender's NDCG through the autoencoder approaches the original — the sparse code loses little of the downstream quality.

> A tool from LLM interpretability, borrowed to make a recommender's memory readable.
slides.notes: Two ideas from the language-model world, transplanted: sparse autoencoders were built to read the internals of LLMs; here they read the internals of a collaborative filter. Nothing in the backbone is retrained. If short on time, say only step three.
slides.summary: Hradil 2026, part one: a TopK sparse autoencoder projects the dense CF user embedding into a wide latent where most features mean one thing.

slides.title: Say it: a sentence becomes a direction in that space
slides.body:
![[fig-steering-pipeline|60%]]

1. For every item, an LLM writes five short requests that describe it **without naming it** — *Toy Story* → "animated buddy adventure for all ages"; requests are split 3 / 1 / 1 per item into train, validation and test — so the test asks whether a **new phrasing** about a known item moves that item: paraphrase steering in an offline probe, not steering toward never-seen items. This closes the request–metadata gap the way HyDE closes the query–document gap in search.
2. A two-layer mapper learns text embedding (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B) → the item's sparse code, trained with **InfoNCE** — a retrieval objective.
3. Online: embed the request, map it to a direction **δ**, normalise to the user's activation mass, then **blend** `(1−α)·user + α·δ` and re-apply TopK. Mass is normalised to avoid score-scale drift; the effect on ranking quality is measured, not assumed.
4. Decode through the SAE and the CF decoder → a steered ranking. No retraining anywhere.

<!-- gap -->

> The steering request is literally a search query — the training prompt begins "You are a search-query writer".
slides.notes: This is where the convergence thesis appears inside our own work: the recommender is steered by the machinery of semantic search — a text embedder, a contrastive objective, synthetic queries — pointed at the user embedding instead of at documents. The α knob is what a product would expose as a slider. If short on time, keep steps three and four.
slides.summary: Hradil 2026, part two: synthetic requests per item train a small mapper from text embeddings to the sparse latent; at inference the request is blended into the user's code with mass preserved.

slides.title: Offline probe: language moves the ranking on four backbones, most on ELSA
slides.body:
![[fig-steering-alpha|52%]]

| MRR of the requested item, base → best (dataset, backbone) | |
|---|---|
| MIND, **ELSA** | 0.042 → **0.324** — in reciprocal-rank terms, ≈ 24th → ≈ 3rd |
| MIND, ALS | 0.035 → 0.235 |
| MovieLens-25M, ALS | 0.111 → 0.216 — "roughly doubles" |
| MovieLens-25M, ELSA | 0.122 → 0.192 |

Controls: steering toward a **random** other item lowers the target's rank; without the sparse autoencoder the same mapper reaches only 0.144 instead of 0.235 on MIND.

*Evidence level: MSc thesis, offline, no user study; the probe metric credits only the exact item; additive requests only; publication in preparation.*

> Moderate steering enriches the profile with the topic; full steering overwrites it. The dial matters.
slides.notes: Two datasets, four backbones, every configuration improved. The limits belong on the slide as spoken: offline only, no user study, only additive requests — "less action movies" is not handled yet — the probe credits only the exact item, and the requests are paraphrases about known items. ELSA, our linear autoencoder from 2022, is the strongest backbone on news. If short on time, read the ELSA row and the controls.
slides.summary: Hradil 2026 results: on MIND with ELSA the requested item's MRR rises from 0.042 to 0.324 (reciprocal-rank equivalent of 24th to 3rd); a random request pushes it down, so the effect is meaning, not mixing.

slides.title: Where hallucination comes from, and how retrieval closes it
slides.body:
| Failure mode ([RAG survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13193)) | What actually went wrong | Which stage owns it |
|---|---|---|
| **Missing-information hallucination** | the passage with the answer was never retrieved, so the model answers from memory | retrieval, ranking |
| **Cherry-picking under contradiction** | two passages disagree; the model quotes one and ignores the other | ranking, fusion |
| Stale answer | the knowledge is in the weights, not in the index | parametric fusion |
| Unsupported synthesis despite correct evidence | the generator embroiders | generator; faithfulness checker |

**Metric:** *answer faithfulness* — is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? Not fluency, not relevance of the answer to the question.

> A conversational system that hallucinates often has a ranking problem wearing a language-model costume — and a generator that still needs checking.
slides.notes: For an information-systems audience the useful reframing is ownership: most hallucinations in retrieval-augmented systems are attributable to the retrieval and ranking stages the audience already understands, not to the generator. That also says what to measure — groundedness of the answer in the evidence — and where to fix it. If short on time, read the first row and the last line.
slides.summary: Q5: the failure modes of a retrieval-augmented system are retrieval failures first; the metric that matters is faithfulness to the retrieved evidence.

slides.title: Grounding by construction
slides.body:
![[fig-semantic-ids|56%]]

| Guard rail | Mechanism | Guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Prefix trie over semantic IDs ([TIGER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065)) | beam search only follows paths to real items | every recommended item exists |
| Grammar-constrained generation | a grammar masks the next-token distribution | every emitted structure is well-formed |
| Catalogue retrieval before writing (RAG) | the writer sees only ranked evidence; citations chosen from retrieved IDs | provenance — every citation names a retrieved item; whether it supports the claim is a separate faithfulness check |

The remaining risk moves up one level: the item exists, but is it the right one? That is the accuracy question of the next section.

> Constrained decoding is the model-driven-development guard rail, applied to a catalogue.
slides.notes: The bridge to Herwig Mannaert's keynote: guard rails for generated artefacts have an exact counterpart in generative retrieval, where the decoder is restricted to a trie of valid identifiers. It converts "the model rarely invents products" into "the model cannot invent products". What it cannot do is choose well — which is why the talk turns to evaluation next. If short on time, keep the first row and the last line. Bridge: existence is not relevance. Grounding guarantees the system points at something real; the next section asks how we would know it pointed at the right thing.
slides.summary: Constrained decoding over the catalogue: the model can only emit identifiers that exist, so a class of fabrication is impossible rather than unlikely.

slides.title: Are we really making progress? 2019 and 2026
slides.body:
![[fig-reproducibility-funnel|50%]]

| | RecSys 2019 best paper ([Ferrari Dacrema et al.](https://doi.org/10.1145/3298689.3347058)) | ACM TORS 2026 ([Benigni et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09364)) |
|---|---|---|
| Sample | 18 neural top-n methods, KDD/SIGIR/WWW/RecSys 2015–18 | 9 diffusion recommenders, SIGIR 2023–24 |
| Reproducible | **7 of 18** with reasonable effort | **25 %** of reported results |
| Against tuned simple baselines | **6 of 7** beaten by kNN or graph methods | DiffRec ≈ ItemKNN, a 25-year-old method; beaten by RP3β, iALS, GF-CF |

> Seven years apart, the same finding: an untuned baseline makes any architecture look like progress.
slides.notes: Two studies from the same Politecnico di Milano group, and the second one is more damning because the field had been warned. The mechanism is not fraud; it is that offline evaluation on public datasets rewards whoever tunes their own model hardest. For the audience the lesson is procedural: a strong, tuned, cheap baseline belongs in every comparison — which is also why linear models keep reappearing in this talk. If short on time, read the two bottom rows.
slides.summary: The reproducibility crisis, twice: neural recommenders in 2019, diffusion recommenders in 2026; same disease, different architecture.

slides.title: The proxy ladder
slides.body:
![[fig-proxy-ladder|52%]]

| Rung | Cost | What it can miss |
|---|---|---|
| NDCG@10 over 999 sampled negatives | minutes | exposure bias; the sampling itself changes the ranking of methods |
| Full-catalogue ranking | hours | still measures resemblance to the logged policy |
| Simulated users, LLM judges | days | the simulator inherits the priors of the model that powers it |
| Online A/B test | weeks, real users | long-term effects, novelty decay |
| Long-term value | quarters | — |

Evidence for the gaps: NDCG and Recall "frequently fail to correlate strongly with online A/B test results" ([Ziabari et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11493)); a context-aware simulator is validated against **55 real A/B tests** rather than trusted ([ContextSim, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09549)).

Academia built rungs in between — sampled-metric theory (Krichene and Rendle, KDD 2020), reproducibility frameworks (RecBole, Elliot), off-policy estimators. And the top rung is not truth either: A/B tests are short, noisy and blind to interference (Kohavi, Tang and Xu, 2020).

> A proxy is only as good as its measured correlation with the rung above it — and that includes the A/B test.
slides.notes: The organising picture for the accuracy axis. Academic papers live on the bottom rung because it is the only one they can afford; production lives on the A/B rung because it is the only one that pays. The new middle rungs — simulators and language-model judges — are promising exactly when they are calibrated against A/B outcomes, and dangerous when they are trusted on their own. If short on time, keep the figure and the last line.
slides.summary: Every evaluation is a proxy for the one above it: sampled offline metrics, full-catalogue ranking, simulators and LLM judges, the A/B test, long-term value. Each step down is cheaper and less true.

slides.title: What production optimises
slides.body:
| System | Offline lift | Online lift | What shipped it |
|---|---|---|---|
| [HSTU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152), Meta 2024 | up to +65.8 % NDCG on public data | "improve metrics in online A/B tests by **12.4 %**" (metric not named) | a model "three orders of magnitude more computationally complex" served at 1.5–3× throughput (M-FALCON) |
| [OneRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695), Kuaishou 2025 | — | App Stay Time **+0.54 % / +1.24 %** | OPEX **10.6 %** of the cascade; MFU 23.7 % / 28.8 % |
| [UniPinRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00422), Pinterest 2026 | Hit@3 **+14.8 %** | **~+1 %** engagement | latency −11.1 %, QPS +63.6 % |
| [GLIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17540), Spotify 2026 | Recall@30 +29.5 % vs text-conditioned variant | non-habitual streams **+5.4 %** | within production cost and latency |
| [PinFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704), Pinterest 2025 | — | engagement with new items up | serving throughput **+600 %** (DCAT kernel) |

*Evidence level: industrial papers; metrics differ by row and are not comparable; baselines non-public; successes are what gets published.*

> Offline lift is a hypothesis. The A/B test is the shared production measurement of a chosen proxy — stay time is a proxy too. The cost column is the decision.
slides.notes: Read the Pinterest row aloud: a fourteen-percent offline gain became a one-percent online gain, and the paper is still a success because it cut latency and raised throughput. Read the Kuaishou row: the model costs ten times the FLOPs and a tenth of the money, because a single model uses the GPUs the cascade left idle. These are the figures an academic paper does not report and an information-systems team cannot do without. If short on time, read only the last line and the Pinterest row.
slides.summary: The numbers deployed systems report: offline lift, online lift, and the cost or latency figure that actually shipped the system.

slides.title: The same disease one floor down: backbone isolation
slides.body:
![[fig-reef|42%]]

**The problem.** Two teams compare encoders for recommendation and disagree. The difference could come from the backbone, the embedding size, the downstream ranker, the budget or the split — and practice does not separate them.

**REEF** (Recommender Embedding Evaluation Framework, Tomáš Laurin, CTU 2026): one loader, one task, one downstream ranker, one evaluator; **only the backbone changes.** Eight encoders including a non-semantic baseline, three catalogues, five scenarios: 120 cells.

**Independent confirmation.** Snap's [GRID handbook](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22224) (CIKM 2025): "varied modeling techniques, hyper-parameters and experimental setups … make direct comparisons challenging" — and components the literature overlooks change the result.

*Evidence level: MSc thesis, offline; REEF reports sampled-negative metrics (999 negatives) for tractability — the contribution is the protocol, full-catalogue validation is future work; GRID is peer-reviewed and open source.*

> 2019 could not compare models. 2026 cannot compare encoders. Two groups answered with a framework in the same year.
slides.notes: This is where our lab's work sits on the accuracy axis: not a better model, a better measurement. REEF is protocol-based — task, backbone, trainer, downstream model, evaluator are interfaces — so a claim about an encoder is a claim about the encoder. Status: thesis defended May 2026; publication in preparation. If short on time, read the problem paragraph and the last line.
slides.summary: Laurin 2026 names the backbone isolation problem and answers it with REEF; Snap's GRID reached the same diagnosis for generative recommenders in the same year.

slides.title: A robust pattern: content helps most when behaviour is missing
slides.body:
![[fig-coldstart-result|52%]]

| Evidence | Cold items | Warm items |
|---|---|---|
| [A-LLMRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11343), KDD 2024 | LLM- and modality-based models beat SASRec | **SASRec beats them back** |
| REEF zero-shot (Laurin 2026), Recall@10 over 999 sampled negatives | the non-semantic baseline falls to the random floor (≈ 0.01) while GTE-base reaches 0.234 on MovieLens; **every** pretrained encoder stays above the floor | text wins on MovieLens and Amazon, image and multimodal win on H&M fashion |
| [TIGER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05065) | a content-derived ID gives new items a place in the model | — |
| [FilterLLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16924), 2025 | one forward pass emits a distribution over users for a new item instead of hundreds of yes/no prompts | — |

> Content encoders give a semantic prior; interactions give behaviour. A pattern across these papers and our own results, not a law — and a system should know which one it is missing.
slides.notes: The regularity holds from benchmarks to production: content representations are structurally the difference between something and nothing at cold start, and collaborative signal wins as soon as history exists. REEF adds the nuance that the winning modality depends on what carries preference in the catalogue — titles for films, images for clothes. The next section is about paying for both. If short on time, read the first two rows.
slides.summary: The cleanest empirical regularity across the literature: language and image models beat collaborative filtering on new items and lose to it on items with history.

slides.title: What a query costs at a hundred million users
slides.body:
![[fig-latency-budget|52%]]

| Constraint | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **> 400,000 requests per second, < 500 ms** | Kuaishou's stated envelope for its recommender ([OneRec report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695)) |
| **≈ 100 ms** end-to-end for a synchronous recommendation surface | an example product budget: retrieval, features, ranker, constraints and network share it |
| Thousands of tokens per request | what a language model costs when it is on the request path |

Illustrative arithmetic (September 2026 list prices for a hosted model; self-hosting changes the number): 100 M users × 3 sessions × 5 pages = **1.5 billion ranking calls a day**. Put a language model on that path at 1,000 tokens a call and $0.10 per million tokens: **$150,000 a day** for the generation step alone, before retrieval, and before any cache hit. A dot product costs microseconds.

> Cost per request is a learning objective, not an operations detail.
slides.notes: The affordability axis in one arithmetic sentence. The Kuaishou envelope is quoted from their own report: recommenders "are often constrained to operate at a low scale and are not computation-intensive" because of QPS and latency. In our own taxonomy of objectives, cost efficiency and sub-100-millisecond response are goals of the learning problem, not something the infrastructure team fixes later. If short on time, read the first row and the last line.
slides.summary: Q6 opener: the budget nobody negotiates — QPS, latency, and the fact that a recommender request is a dot product while a language-model request is thousands of tokens.

slides.title: Compute versus value
slides.body:
![[fig-scaling-laws|48%]]

| | [HSTU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) (Meta, 2024) | [OneRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695) (Kuaishou, 2025) |
|---|---|---|
| Model change | 1.5 trillion parameters; "three orders of magnitude more computationally complex than prior state-of-the-art" — model complexity, not production cost | one end-to-end model replacing the cascade, ~10× its FLOPs |
| Business effect | "improve metrics in online A/B tests by 12.4 %" (metric not named) | App Stay Time +0.54 % / +1.24 % |
| Why it was affordable | M-FALCON amortises a 285× more complex model at 1.5–3× throughput | model-FLOPs utilisation 23.7 % / 28.8 % — the cascade had left the GPUs idle |

> In Kuaishou's accounting the saving came from using the hardware, not from a smarter model — and the migration cost is not in the report.
slides.notes: Both papers claim a scaling law; the difference is in the fine print. Economic intuition, not from the paper: a platform with billions of users can afford a thousandfold model complexity for twelve percent. Kuaishou's more interesting message for this audience is systemic: fragmenting the work into four stages wasted the accelerators, and a single model at ten times the FLOPs cost a tenth as much to run. Neither paper reports the migration cost of rebuilding the stack, and nobody has. If short on time, read the last row.
slides.summary: The scaling law arrived in recommendation, and so did its bill: Meta's HSTU paid three orders of magnitude of compute for +12.4 %; Kuaishou's OneRec paid ten times the FLOPs and a tenth of the money.

slides.title: Four serving levers
slides.body:
![[fig-serving-tricks|50%]]

| Lever | System | Reported effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Cache the user state across requests** (hierarchical KV cache, GPU + host RAM) | [MTServe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22881), 2026 | up to **3.1×** faster, hit ratio > 98.5 % |
| **Reuse the encoding across stages** (retrieval and ranking share one KV cache) | [UniPinRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00422), Pinterest | > 3× ranking forward-pass speedup; −11.1 % latency |
| **Deduplicate attention** over the shared user sequence | [PinFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704), Pinterest | **+600 %** serving throughput, +200 % training |
| **Linear attention + request-level batching** for 10,000-event histories | [Douyin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06077), 2026 | −77–84 % bandwidth; 10k histories at full traffic |

> At scale a modelling win is realised only together with a serving win. Read the systems section of these papers first.
slides.notes: Every row is a systems contribution that unlocked a modelling result. The pattern for an information-systems audience: the user's history is the expensive part of every request, so cache it, share it between stages, and never encode it twice. If short on time, read the first and the last row.
slides.summary: Q7: the tricks that make long histories and big models fit the budget — caches across requests, reuse across stages, deduplicated attention, linear attention with request-level batching.

slides.title: Structure can beat parameter count on the right task
slides.body:
| Result | Source |
|---|---|
| A **0.6 B** model with a dedicated semantic-ID encoder outperforms a **4 B** model without one on SID prediction; deepest-level accuracy +46 % relative | [PrefixMem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00324), Pinterest 2026 |
| A sparse, inverted-index retriever from the same BERT slightly beats its dense sibling (0.322 vs 0.312 MRR@10) | [SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720), 2021 |
| Dense embeddings projected into a high-dimensional, sparsely activated space: **12× fewer parameters** at near-uncompressed quality, beating Matryoshka embeddings of the same size; two inference modes — fast in the sparse space, exact in the reconstructed dense space | **CompresSAE**, Recombee Labs, [RecSys 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11388) |

> "Dense embeddings are a convenient default, but at scale they become one of the most expensive parts." — [Recombee Labs, 2025 research retrospective](https://www.recombee.com/blog/a-2025-research-retrospective)
slides.notes: The affordability answer that does not require a trillion parameters: give the model the right structure. Pinterest's result is the sharpest — semantic IDs are a modality and want an encoder, exactly as images do in multimodal LLMs — and CompresSAE is our version of the same idea for retrieval: sparsity as a design decision, with a latency-versus-quality dial at run time. If short on time, read the first and the last row.
slides.summary: Evidence from three places that structure buys more than parameters: a 0.6-billion model with a semantic-ID encoder beats a 4-billion one without; sparse retrievers match dense; CompresSAE cuts parameters twelvefold.

slides.title: Linear models are not dead
slides.body:
![[fig-ease-vs-elsa|44%]]

| | [EASE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.03375) (Netflix, 2019) | **ELSA** (Recombee Labs, [RecSys 2022](https://doi.org/10.1145/3523227.3551482)) |
|---|---|---|
| Model | a dense item–item matrix, closed form, negatives allowed | the hidden layer factorised into low-rank plus sparse |
| Cost | O(items²) memory — ten million items squared at 32-bit is about 400 TB of weights | **O(items · d)** — the item–item matrix is never materialised |
| Accuracy | strongest simple baseline in the field | **beats EASE** on several tasks; industrial validation in ACM TORS 2025 |
| Where | MovieLens | production, catalogues of tens of millions of items; successor **SANSA** deployed |

> Keep a strong linear baseline. This is what happens when somebody does that honestly for three years: the embarrassing baseline becomes infrastructure.
slides.notes: The line from the reproducibility slide to our lab: the methods that kept beating neural recommenders in 2019 were linear, and the reason nobody deployed the best of them was a quadratic matrix. ELSA — Vančura, Alves, Kasalický and Kordík, RecSys 2022 — factorises that layer, scales linearly in the catalogue and is more accurate, not merely cheaper. "It is quite difficult to overfit training data with linear models." If short on time, read the cost row and the last line.
slides.summary: EASE was the strongest simple baseline and could not be deployed; ELSA made it scale and beat it; SANSA runs it in production.

slides.title: beeFormer: interaction data inside the text encoder
slides.body:
![[fig-beeformer|66%]]

- A sentence Transformer ([Sentence-BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) lineage) encodes item text; the **ELSA** objective reconstructs users' interaction vectors through the item–item operator; the gradient reaches the encoder.
- One encoder whose vectors understand both what an item **is** and what people **do** with it: cold-start and zero-shot, and transfer across domains — train on books, recommend films.
- Training on several domains accumulates knowledge in one model. Open source: [github.com/recombee/beeformer](https://github.com/recombee/beeformer) · paper [arXiv:2409.10309](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.10309).

> ELSA stopped being only a model. It became a loss function you can use to train something else entirely.
slides.notes: The mechanism behind the "semantic is not behavioural" slide, from our side: NoteLLM at Xiaohongshu and Recformer do the same thing with a large language model; beeFormer does it with a small sentence encoder and a linear loss, which is the affordable way. If short on time, keep the figure and the last line.
slides.summary: RecSys 2024: let the recommendation loss — ELSA — flow back into a sentence Transformer, so one encoder reads both text and behaviour.

slides.title: In our REEF protocol, the strongest objective was the 2022 linear loss
slides.body:
![[fig-winning-config|52%]]

| Recall@10, frozen → fine-tuned (BGE-M3 + SigLIP2) | Standard | Cold start |
|---|---|---|
| MovieLens 20M | 0.301 → 0.349 (**+15.9 %**) | +13.7 % |
| H&M Fashion | 0.164 → 0.211 (**+28.7 %**) | +23.4 % |
| Amazon Reviews 2023 | 0.121 → 0.154 (**+27.3 %**) | **+39.0 %** |

- **LoRA** beats full fine-tuning everywhere; on Amazon full fine-tuning is *worse than the frozen encoder* (0.121 → 0.115).
- **ELSA** beats BPR, InfoNCE, Jaccard and PMI as the objective; ELSA + InfoNCE together collapse (0.323 → 0.245).
- **Honest negative:** four of six cross-domain and cross-dataset transfer settings stay at the random-ranker floor.

*Evidence level: MSc thesis, offline, sampled-negative Recall@10 (999 negatives), publication in preparation.*

> In 2024 we put interaction data inside the text encoder. In 2026 we generalised it to images — and the best way to do it is still the linear loss from 2022.
slides.notes: Tomáš Laurin's thesis, defended May 2026, generalises beeFormer to text plus image with a frozen backbone, low-rank adapters and a learned per-item fusion, and finds that the ELSA reconstruction loss aligns the embedding geometry with collaborative behaviour while keeping enough semantic structure for cold start. State the failures too: the transfer columns are floor-to-floor, and the thesis says so. This is the affordability answer — you do not need 1.5 trillion parameters, you need a frozen backbone, LoRA and the right objective. If short on time, read the table and the last line. Bridge: the cheaper and more unified the stack becomes, the more power one ranking decision has — which turns control, safety, exposure and audit into first-class requirements. That is the next section.
slides.summary: Laurin 2026, fine-tuning multimodal encoders on interactions under REEF: LoRA + interaction-conditioned attention fusion + ELSA wins; full fine-tuning damages the pretrained space; transfer mostly fails.

slides.title: Alignment is a table of measurable properties
slides.body:
| Property | The question | Metric | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Controllable** | can the user move it where they want? | rank of the requested item (MRR) | natural-language steering of the user embedding |
| **Safe** | what does it let through, leak or do? | harmful-query accuracy; leakage and policy tests | moderation + retrieval filtering + output and action constraints + audit |
| **Fair exposure** | who gets seen? | exposure share of items and suppliers | minimum-exposure guarantees, re-ranking |
| **Calibrated** | does my 4 mean your 4? | rating-level consistency across users | user-specific discretisation of a shared semantic scale |
| **Evaluable** | is the judge better than the proxy? | correlation with A/B outcomes | behaviourally aligned judges and simulators |

> Every row is engineering: a number to move, a component that moves it.
slides.notes: The definition the annotation asked for — alignment for an engineer — as a table rather than a philosophy. Each row is unpacked on the following slides, and each has a paper from our lab or from the literature behind it. If short on time, read the property column only.
slides.summary: Q8 opener: for an engineer, alignment is not a model's mood; it is five properties, each with a metric and a mechanism, each with a production example.

slides.title: Convergence merges vulnerabilities: SHIELD
slides.body:
![[fig-shield|46%]]

| Query | Keyword filter | Semantic retrieval |
|---|---|---|
| "glass tubing" | passes — no blocked word | returns laboratory equipment with an obvious illicit use |
| a harmful request phrased without any blocked word | passes | understood, and answered |

**SHIELD** (Recombee Labs, UMAP 2025): hierarchical LLM-generated queries → reward-model filtering → classifier. Marketplace evaluation, 17,170 harmful and 8,871 sensitive queries:

| Accuracy on the marketplace test set | BM25 keyword similarity | Semantic embeddings + FAISS | **MoralBERT, fine-tuned** |
|---|---|---|---|
| harmful vs. sensitive queries | 93.2 % | 96.5 % | **98.4 %** (F1 98.6 %) |

> Merge the stacks and you merge the attack surface. The fix has to understand meaning as well as the search does.
slides.notes: Our own evidence that convergence is not free: the moment search became semantic, the keyword blocklists that had protected marketplaces for a decade stopped working. SHIELD builds the training data hierarchically, filters it with a reward model and trains a small classifier that sits in the moderation layer. Presented at UMAP 2025 in New York; blog post on recombee.com. If short on time, read the two example queries and the 98.4 %.
slides.summary: Semantic search understands meaning, so harmful queries walk around keyword filters; SHIELD is the dataset and classifier that closes the gap.

slides.title: Exposure and the feedback loop
slides.body:
![[fig-feedback-loop|58%]]

| Finding | Source |
|---|---|
| A recommend → click → retrain loop amplifies popularity bias, shrinks catalogue coverage and homogenises profiles; the minority user group loses most precision | Mansoury, PhD thesis 2021 ([arXiv:2111.05564](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05564)) |
| Seven named biases enter at three points — data, model, results — and the loop feeds them back | [Chen et al., bias and debias survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03240) |
| Web-search diversification (xQuAD) and fair top-k ranking reused as recommender re-rankers | same thesis — the post-processing slot is shared across interfaces |
| **Minimum item exposure guarantees**: eligible items get an exposure floor, with a measured relevance trade-off | Recombee Labs, 2024 — [blog](https://www.recombee.com/blog/making-recommendations-fairer-a-new-way-to-guarantee-exposure-for-all) |

> Bias is not a property of the data. It is a property of the loop the system closes on itself.
slides.notes: The alignment topic an information-systems audience can act on: exposure is a resource the system allocates, and a floor on it is a constraint you can enforce at re-ranking time — Recombee's minimum-exposure work does exactly that for multi-supplier catalogues. The thesis result on minority users is the one to say aloud. If short on time, read the first and the last row.
slides.summary: The model learns only from what it showed; the loop amplifies popularity, shrinks coverage and hurts minority users most; exposure guarantees are the engineering answer.

slides.title: Evaluation is alignment: judges need behavioural alignment too
slides.body:
![[fig-circular-evaluation|58%]]

**Bidirectional rationalisation** ([Ziabari et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11493)): in zero-shot, an LLM "convincingly argues for both positive and negative user engagement outcomes on the exact same item with identical evidence".

| Judge | MacroF1 on real homepage interaction logs |
|---|---|
| zero-shot LLM | baseline |
| behaviourally aligned LLM (fine-tuning + preference optimisation over paired rationales) | **+32.19 %**, matches the production feature-engineered model |

A simulator earns trust the same way: ContextSim is checked against 55 real A/B experiments, not against its own plausibility.

> A judge that can argue either way is not a judge. Align it to behaviour, then measure the correlation.
slides.notes: The bridge between the accuracy and alignment axes: the tools that promise to replace offline metrics — language-model judges, agent simulators — have to be aligned to observed behaviour and validated against A/B outcomes before they are allowed to rank models. The failure mode has a name now, which makes it easier to ask a vendor about. If short on time, read the quote and the last line.
slides.summary: Off-the-shelf LLM judges argue convincingly for both outcomes on the same evidence; fine-tuning with preference optimisation over correct and counterfactual rationales fixes it and matches a production feature baseline.

slides.title: The rules outside the model
slides.body:
| Rule | What it asks of a recommender | Which slide answers it |
|---|---|---|
| **DSA, Article 27** | state the main parameters of the recommender system in plain language, and let users influence them | Controllable — steering by language |
| **DSA, Article 38** | very large platforms must offer at least one option not based on profiling | Exposure guarantees; a non-personalised ranking path |
| **AI Act, Article 50** | transparency obligations for AI-generated content | Grounding — cited evidence; audit trail |

> Regulation is arriving as a list of properties. The engineering table four slides ago is the same list.
slides.notes: Keep this short and factual. Dates deliberately stay off the slide: check the AI Act implementation timeline for Article 50 the week of the talk and say it aloud. The point for information-systems developers: the properties the regulator names — explainable parameters, user control, transparency of generated output — are the rows of the alignment table, which means compliance is an engineering deliverable, not a legal appendix. If short on time, drop this slide entirely.
slides.summary: Two European obligations turn alignment properties into requirements: the DSA asks recommenders to explain their main parameters and offer user control; the AI Act adds transparency duties for generated content.

slides.title: The fourth interface: the consumer of the ranking changes
slides.body:
![[fig-agentic-protocols|60%]]

| What changed | What did not |
|---|---|
| Five agent-commerce protocols in nine months (Apr 2025 – Jan 2026); the pattern settling on *discover in the chat, transact on the merchant site* | the catalogue still has to be retrieved from, ranked and constrained |
| Structured attributes and current inventory make items easier for an agent to retrieve, compare and safely transact | the winner is still the best-ranked item — for a new kind of requester |

> Search, recommendation, conversation — and now an agent asks the same question on the user's behalf.
slides.notes: The future section stays on the thesis: agents are not a new stack, they are a new client of the existing one. The commercial protocol race is context, not argument, and it dates fastest — cut it first when short on time. What matters for developers is the last row: structured, machine-readable catalogues are what agents can act on, which is Jakub Klímek's keynote seen from inside the product.
slides.summary: Q9: for the first time the entity reading the ranked list is not a person but an agent acting on a person's behalf; the ranking job is the same, the requester is new.

slides.title: Agents over the same stack
slides.body:
![[fig-mcp-two-products|52%]]

`retrieve candidates → rank actions → apply constraints → execute a tool → audit the outcome` — the taxonomy of the [LLM-agents survey for recommendation and search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05659): the shared pipeline with an execution step. Our agent interface is a Model Context Protocol server — authenticated tool access for agents — in two variants:

| | Developer agent | User's agent |
|---|---|---|
| Who authenticates | the customer of the vendor | the end user, through the merchant's identity provider |
| Scope | the whole database | **one user, read-only**; feedback is the only write |
| Threat model | account misuse | leakage of other people's data, prompt injection, spam |

> The user id comes from the token, never from a parameter — an agent cannot forget to validate what it cannot pass.
slides.notes: Our own design for an agent interface to a recommender, split into two products because the threat models differ. The design decision worth repeating to systems developers is the last line: identity is bound to the credential, so the tool has no parameter through which an agent could ask about someone else. The agent loop itself is the ranking pipeline with an execution stage; alignment properties — constraints, audit — are where the engineering effort goes. If short on time, keep the table and the last line.
slides.summary: An agent loop is retrieve → rank actions → constrain → execute → audit; the Recombee MCP design shows the one thing that must change — who authenticates, and what the agent is allowed to see.

slides.title: Structured catalogue plus guard rails
slides.body:
| Keynote | Their theme | The same theme inside a ranking system |
|---|---|---|
| **Jakub Klímek** — semantic data interoperability, DCAT-AP, data spaces | structured, machine-readable data between organisations | a structured catalogue is what embeddings, semantic IDs and agents are computed from; its quality bounds everything downstream |
| **Herwig Mannaert** — guard rails for generation in model-driven development | controlled, sustainable AI generation | constrained decoding over a trie of valid identifiers; retrieval before writing; audit of what was shown |

> An agentic interface does not lower the bar for the catalogue. It is the first client that refuses to work without one.
slides.notes: A deliberate tie to the conference programme so the audience hears one story across three keynotes. Both connections are literal, not rhetorical: semantic IDs are computed from catalogue attributes, and constrained decoding is a grammar over the catalogue. If short on time, read the last line.
slides.summary: The two other keynotes of this conference, seen from inside the product: a machine-readable catalogue is the precondition, constrained decoding is the guard rail.

slides.title: A lab wired into production
slides.body:
![[fig-research-loop|60%]]

`production question → research method → measured result → deployed feature` — two loops that closed:

| Loop | Production problem | Method | Result | Feature |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Safety** | semantic search let harmful queries past keyword filters | SHIELD: generated hierarchical queries, reward-model filtering, small classifier | 98.4 % accuracy on the marketplace test set | a moderation layer in front of semantic search |
| **Scale** | the best linear model (EASE) needed a quadratic matrix | ELSA: factorise the hidden layer | linear cost, more accurate than EASE | production for catalogues of tens of millions of items; SANSA after it |

Open source: **ELSA · beeFormer · CompresSAE · Repsys** — [github.com/recombee](https://github.com/recombee). Principle: personalisation with genuine user value, not ad targeting.

> The lab's advantage is not size. It is data access: prototypes are A/B-tested where the users are.
slides.notes: Recombee: founded 2015 in Prague, six co-founders, four with doctorates; RecombeeLab is the joint laboratory with the Department of Applied Mathematics at CTU FIT; 15 peer-reviewed publications in 2025 (say it, do not show it). Operational figures — over ten thousand sites and apps, over a billion recommendations a day — are public marketing numbers: verify against internal reporting before quoting them aloud. The point for the audience is methodological: the question comes from traffic, the answer goes back to traffic. If short on time, read the loop line and the last line.
slides.summary: Q10: Recombee Labs is a joint CTU–Recombee laboratory with A/B access to live traffic across thousands of catalogues; the loop from production question to paper to feature is the method.

slides.title: Four threads, one question
slides.body:
![[fig-portfolio|60%]]

| Axis | Flagship | One result |
|---|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | REEF — compare encoders with everything else held still | in one protocol, a frozen encoder plus LoRA and the ELSA loss: Recall@10 +16–29 % |
| **Affordability** | ELSA and CompresSAE — linear and sparse by design | linear cost, more accurate than EASE; embeddings with 12× fewer parameters |
| **Alignment** | SHIELD and language steering — safety and control as numbers | 98.4 % harmful-query accuracy; the requested item from ≈ 24th to ≈ 3rd |

> Frontier labs work on being better. We have spent ten years on being good enough within a budget somebody will approve. That is a different question — and it is the one more people have.
slides.notes: The portfolio in one table so nothing is a surprise, and the sentence that positions it. Each thread maps to an axis of the talk: sparsity and representation to affordability, trustworthiness to alignment, evaluation to accuracy. If short on time, read only the last line.
slides.summary: Every publication answers one question: how to get large-model quality into a budget an ordinary company can approve.

slides.title: Where this goes: controllable, evaluable, safe
slides.body:
![[fig-whats-next|60%]]

Conversational and agentic recommender systems that "plan and adapt sequences of actions while staying **controllable, evaluable, and safe**."

| Word | What it already means here |
|---|---|
| **controllable** | steering by language (Hradil), constrained decoding, business rules as a query language |
| **evaluable** | REEF, offline-to-online correlation, behaviourally aligned judges |
| **safe** | SHIELD, exposure guarantees, an agent interface that cannot ask about another user |

> Two theses from this year already sit on that line: one makes the recommender listen, the other makes it measurable.
slides.notes: Rodrigo Alves's stated research direction, quoted, and mapped back to the talk so the future is not a wish list. The two theses — Jaroslav Hradil's steering and Tomáš Laurin's REEF — are the first concrete steps; both were defended in May 2026, and both are being prepared for publication. If short on time, read the quote and the last line.
slides.summary: The lab's direction for 2026 in our Head of Research's words, and how each word maps to something already shown.

slides.title: Three axes, three sentences
slides.body:
![[fig-three-axes-full|64%]]

| Axis | The sentence |
|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | Offline metrics are hypotheses; the A/B test is the measurement; and even encoders cannot be compared until everything else is held still. |
| **Affordability** | Cost per request is a learning objective — and the cheapest good model is usually structured, sparse or linear, not large. |
| **Alignment** | Controllable, safe, fair, calibrated, evaluable: five numbers to move, five components that move them. |

> Four interfaces, one shared subroutine: choose a few things from a catalogue and put them in order. Everything else is what that costs, whose objective it serves, and whether it was the right order.
slides.notes: Return to the one sentence of the opening and place every section on the three axes. Then stop. If short on time, this is the slide to end on regardless of what was skipped.
slides.summary: The close: the whole talk placed on the three axes from the annotation.
